name: HouseBench
description: Intelligent-building research has hardware, and it has decision layers, and almost no way of telling whether a given architecture keeps a dwelling habitable once the dwelling changes. This paper supplies both halves. The first is a reference architecture, stated completely enough to implement: eleven layers, an ontology of 46 machine-readable classes each carrying seven fields, an entity model whose tenth field is provenance, one reversible interface with 5 channels and an 8-question handshake, perception measured eight separate ways, an 11-step runtime loop with the safety filter inside it, and eight invariants below everything that reasons. The second is HouseBench: 12 procedurally generated dwellings, seven architectures, 15 adversarial tasks, a removal ladder of 6 rungs, 16 quantities measured separately, and 882 logged runs. The headline result is uncomfortable for everybody, this author included. With nothing broken every architecture above a commissioned table performs alike. Separation arrives under injury, and it is separation by dependence: the centre removed takes three architectures from 38 per cent of the day to 0 per cent; carriage cut takes the coordinated system to 0 per cent; and a confident wrong reading leaves six of seven at 8 per cent against 38 per cent for the one carrying provenance and a command log. On eight plans nobody tuned against, a commissioned table holds 0 per cent.
